questions.question: What is a Prompt?
questions.answer:
A prompt is any input—text, code, question, or command—that you provide to an AI model. It's essentially the starting point of the AI's response. For example:

"Summarize this article in 100 words."
"Generate a Python script to scrape headlines from a news site."

Learn by Iterating: Start with a simple prompt, refine it, and compare results.
Study Examples: Explore prompt libraries or communities like PromptBase.
Combine with APIs: If you're technical, practice sending prompts via API calls.
Build a Portfolio: Document your best prompts and outcomes for future reference.

Prompt engineering is about maximizing the value of AI outputs. Clarity, context, and iteration are the foundations. It's a blend of communication, creativity, and technical understanding. As AI becomes ubiquitous, prompt engineering will be a core digital skill.

AI prompt engineering is not just a buzzword—it's a practical, high-impact skill. Whether you're a marketer, tester, developer, or business leader, knowing how to "speak AI" effectively can give you a significant edge. In a world where AI models are the new tools of productivity and creativity, prompt engineering is your interface to unlock their full potential.

questions.question: What is Prompt Engineering in AI?
questions.answer:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming industries, and one of the key skills enabling this transformation is prompt engineering. As large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and others become more capable, the quality of their output increasingly depends on how we interact with them. This interaction happens through prompts—the instructions we give to AI systems.

Prompt engineering has emerged as a critical discipline that focuses on designing, refining, and optimizing these prompts to get desired, reliable, and high-quality outputs from AI models.

questions.question: Why Prompt Engineering Matters
questions.answer:
AI models are powerful but not magical. The same model can produce dramatically different answers depending on how you ask. Prompt engineering helps to:

Improve Accuracy: Well-structured prompts reduce irrelevant or incorrect responses.
Save Time: Good prompts mean fewer retries, edits, or clarifications.
Enhance Creativity: Prompts can push AI to generate innovative ideas, designs, or solutions.
Ensure Consistency: Standardized prompts create uniform outputs, essential for businesses and teams.

In short, prompt engineering maximizes the value of AI while minimizing risks of poor output.

questions.question: How Prompt Engineering Works
questions.answer:
Effective prompt engineering involves several principles:

Clarity & Specificity
Clear instructions lead to clearer outputs.
Example: Instead of "Explain AI," ask "Explain artificial intelligence in 200 words suitable for a 12-year-old."

Context & Role Assignment
Giving the AI a role (teacher, developer, marketer) shapes its tone and approach.
Example: "You are an experienced HR manager. Draft a job description for a QA tester."

Step-by-Step Instructions
Breaking complex tasks into steps improves reliability.
Example: "List the top 5 risks of AI adoption. Then explain how to mitigate each."

Constraints & Formats
Define the desired format (bullet points, tables, code, JSON, etc.).
Example: "Provide the output in a markdown table with columns: Feature, Benefit, and Risk."

Iterative Refinement: Prompt engineering is rarely one-and-done. Testing, refining, and experimenting improve results.

questions.question: What are the Types of Prompts?
questions.answer:
Prompt engineering is not one-size-fits-all. Common prompt categories include:

• Instructional Prompts: "Write a LinkedIn post about AI testing."
• Creative Prompts: "Generate a story about a robot learning empathy."
• Analytical Prompts: "Compare Selenium and Playwright in a table."
• Code Generation Prompts: "Write a Python function to calculate compound interest."
• Multi-turn Prompts: Building on previous answers to refine output.

questions.question: What is Prompt Engineering Defined?
questions.answer:
Prompt engineering is the art and science of crafting effective prompts to guide an AI model toward producing accurate, context-relevant, and high-quality responses. It blends linguistic clarity, domain expertise, and an understanding of the AI model's behavior.

Think of prompt engineering as a conversation skill—but instead of with humans, it's with AI. The better you are at asking, the better the answers you receive.

• Enterprise Use: Organizations now develop prompt libraries or prompt templates to ensure consistent and high-quality use of AI across teams. Tools like LangChain and PromptLayer help manage and optimize prompts at scale.

questions.question: What is the Future of Prompt Engineering?

• Hybrid Roles: "Prompt engineers" merging with "AI product managers" or "AI strategists."

While some believe prompt engineering will become less critical as models improve, others see it as a core skill of the AI-first workforce—similar to knowing how to use search engines or spreadsheets.

questions.question: What is an LLM (Large Language Model)?
questions.answer:
At its core, an LLM (Large Language Model) is an AI system trained to understand, generate, and manipulate human language. These models are built using machine learning, specifically deep learning techniques, and trained on enormous datasets of text from books, articles, websites, code, and more.

"Large" refers to the size of the model, often measured in the number of parameters (weights inside the model). For context:

• GPT-2 had 1.5 billion parameters.
• GPT-3 expanded to 175 billion.
• Newer LLMs like GPT-4 and beyond are even larger, though exact sizes are sometimes undisclosed.

"Language Model" refers to the AI's ability to predict the next word in a sequence based on the words that came before. By repeating this prediction process, the model can generate coherent paragraphs, answer questions, or even write software code.

• Integration Everywhere: From smartphones to enterprise software, LLMs will be embedded into daily tools.

questions.question: What are the Capabilities of LLMs?
questions.answer:
Modern LLMs are extremely versatile. Some of the common applications include:

• Information Retrieval: Acting like a more conversational search engine.
• Education: Tutoring students, explaining concepts, or generating practice problems.

questions.question: How Do LLMs Work?
questions.answer:
LLMs are powered by neural networks, especially a type called transformers. Transformers, introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need", revolutionized NLP (Natural Language Processing) because they could handle long sequences of text with greater accuracy and efficiency.

The process can be broken down as:

• Training: The model is exposed to billions of text samples. It learns patterns, grammar, facts, reasoning steps, and associations between words.
• Fine-Tuning: After general training, the model can be specialized for certain tasks (like answering questions, summarizing text, or coding assistance).
• Inference (Using the Model): When a user types a prompt, the model uses probability to generate the most likely and contextually appropriate next words.

A key innovation is attention mechanisms, which allow the model to "focus" on the most relevant words in a sentence instead of processing everything equally. This helps it maintain coherence in long texts.

questions.question: The Role of Testers in the AI Era
questions.answer:
One of the biggest myths is that AI will replace testers. In reality, AI will replace repetitive and low-value tasks, freeing testers to focus on areas where human creativity, intuition, and critical thinking are irreplaceable. In 2026, successful testers are those who can:

• Understand AI tool capabilities and limitations
• Interpret AI-generated results correctly
• Collaborate with developers to improve AI accuracy
• Use AI insights for better exploratory testing

questions.question: How Does AI Work in Software Testing?
questions.answer:
The core idea is to use machine learning algorithms, NLP (Natural Language Processing), and computer vision in different parts of the testing lifecycle.

Here are some common applications:

a) Test Case Generation

AI can convert plain English requirements into executable test cases. Example: You feed the tool a user story like, "As a user, I should be able to reset my password via email verification", and it generates the test scenarios, edge cases, and even automation scripts.

b) Self-Healing Test Automation

When an application's UI changes — for example, a button label changes from "Login" to "Sign In" — traditional scripts break. AI-based automation tools can detect such changes and update locators dynamically without human intervention.

c) Predictive Defect Analysis

By studying historical bug data, AI can identify high-risk modules in the application. Testers can then focus more effort on these areas, increasing defect detection rates.

d) Visual Testing with Computer Vision

AI-powered visual validation tools can detect pixel-level differences between expected and actual UI layouts — something traditional DOM-based testing can't do reliably.

e) Intelligent Test Prioritization

Instead of running thousands of tests after every code change, AI algorithms can select only the most relevant tests based on impacted code, reducing execution time drastically.

questions.question: What are the Benefits of AI-Assisted Software Testing?
questions.answer:
• Reduced Maintenance Effort: Self-healing tests automatically adapt to UI changes, cutting down script maintenance time.
• Faster Time-to-Market: AI speeds up test generation, prioritization, and execution, enabling faster feedback loops.
• Improved Test Coverage: AI can generate tests for untested areas by analyzing historical execution data and usage analytics.
• Smarter Decision Making: Predictive analytics identify high-risk modules and optimize testing efforts.
• Continuous Learning & Improvement: AI systems get better over time by learning from previous runs, failures, and developer fixes.

questions.question: What are the Key Areas Where AI Assists in Testing (Test Case Generation)?

questions.question: How is AI used in Software Testing tools?

Modern AI testing features range from "self-healing" locators and test generation to visual validation, flaky-test prediction, test prioritization, and even agentic/autonomous test execution. questions.question: What are the realistic limits and risks of AI in testing?
questions.answer:
AI for testing is powerful, but not magical. Key caveats:

• False confidence / hallucinations: generative outputs or suggested fixes can be incorrect; human review and guards remain essential. Industry surveys show many developers still distrust AI outputs and verify results manually.
• Data bias & model brittleness: models trained on limited or non-representative historical test data can miss new failure modes.
• Security & privacy: test data generation must avoid leaking sensitive data; synthetic data techniques must be validated.
• Vendor lock-in & opaque logic: some AI decisions may be hard to inspect; teams should demand transparency and logs for auditability.
• Maintenance of the AI: models need ongoing retraining and tuning as the application evolves — it's not "set and forget."

questions.question: What is the concept of AI-assisted testing?
questions.answer:
AI-assisted testing is not about replacing human testers or existing automation frameworks like Selenium, Cypress, or Playwright. Instead, it augments them.

Think of it as a co-pilot for testers—helping identify missing scenarios, maintaining scripts when the application UI changes, or generating test data automatically. For instance:

If a button label changes from "Submit" to "Send", a traditional Selenium script may fail. An AI-assisted test tool, however, can use computer vision and contextual understanding to recognize that the button still performs the same action—and self-heal the test script.

That's AI in action—intelligence meeting automation.

questions.question: What are the Key Areas Where AI Assists in Testing (Test Case Prioritization)?
questions.answer:
Machine learning models can predict which tests are most likely to detect new defects based on:

• Code change history
• Past defect data
• Test execution results

This helps testers run the most impactful tests first, saving time in continuous integration pipelines.

questions.question: What are the Challenges and Limitations of AI-Assisted Testing?

• Integration Complexity: Adapting AI tools with existing CI/CD pipelines and frameworks can be complex.
• Human Oversight: AI can assist but not fully replace human judgment, especially in exploratory and usability testing.

questions.question: What is the bottom line for AI in testing?
questions.answer: AI is changing how QA operates — not by replacing skilled testers, but by shifting their work away from repetitive maintenance toward test strategy, exploratory coverage, and quality engineering. The most immediate AI wins are maintenance reduction (self-healing), improved visual coverage, and smarter triage/prioritization. But successful adoption requires realistic expectations, human oversight, strong telemetry, and governance. The market is active and maturing; pilot, measure, and scale where you see clear ROI.

The testers who can use AI effectively and validate AI systems ethically will lead the next generation of quality assurance.

questions.question: Why AI-Powered Testing Matters in 2026
questions.answer:

• Shorter release cycles (thanks to CI/CD and DevOps)
• Increased application complexity (microservices, cloud-native, IoT)
• Growing user expectations for seamless, bug-free experiences
• Multiple device/browser/platform combinations to test

a) Speed Without Compromising Quality

Manual testing and even traditional automation struggle to keep up with daily or hourly releases. AI's ability to generate, prioritize, and maintain test cases automatically means QA teams can test more in less time.

b) Reducing Maintenance Overhead

A big pain in automation is script maintenance. Even small UI changes can break hundreds of tests. With self-healing AI scripts, maintenance time drops significantly, freeing testers to focus on exploratory and creative testing.

c) Early Defect Detection

AI's predictive analytics flag high-risk areas early in the SDLC. This prevents costly post-release bugs and improves developer–tester collaboration.

d) Handling Complex Test Scenarios

Some scenarios — like load testing an AI-driven chatbot, validating real-time IoT data, or testing AR/VR interfaces — are hard to cover with traditional automation. AI's adaptability makes it possible.

e) Empowering Testers with Insights

Instead of just pass/fail reports, AI tools provide actionable insights — such as why a test failed, what code change caused it, and how to prevent similar failures.

questions.question: What are the challenges in AI in Testing?
questions.answer:
• Over-reliance on AI: Testers may blindly trust AI-generated test cases without validation.
• False Positives/Negatives: AI-powered defect prediction can miss certain scenarios.
• Model Training Needs: AI-powered tools themselves require relevant training data to perform optimally.
• Tool Integration: Some AI testing tools are new and may not integrate seamlessly with legacy systems.

questions.question: What are the concrete use-cases of AI in testing (Test prioritization and risk-based testing)?
questions.answer: AI ranks tests by predicted fault-finding value (based on code churn, recent defects, feature criticality, and historical failure rates). CI pipelines can run high-value tests earlier to fail fast and save CI compute.

questions.question: What is AI in Testing?
questions.answer:
AI in Testing refers to the use of Artificial Intelligence techniques, tools, and algorithms to enhance, automate, or optimize the software testing process itself.
Here, AI is a tool for the tester. It doesn't change what you are testing—it changes how you test.

Examples include:

• AI-powered test case generation.
• Predictive analytics for defect detection.
• Intelligent prioritization of regression tests.
• Self-healing test automation scripts.
• AI-driven visual UI testing.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) for converting requirements into automated tests.
In short, AI in Testing is about making testing smarter, faster, and more efficient.

questions.question: What is "AI-assisted" Software Testing?
questions.answer:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has moved far beyond chatbots and recommendation systems. In the world of software testing, it's quietly transforming how QA engineers plan, design, execute, and maintain their tests. AI-assisted software testing refers to the use of machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), and data-driven algorithms to help testers improve test coverage, speed up execution, and make smarter decisions throughout the testing lifecycle.

Unlike traditional automation—where testers explicitly define every step of what to test—AI-assisted testing introduces intelligence and adaptability. The system learns from past data, recognizes patterns, and even predicts where defects are most likely to occur.

questions.question: What are the Key Areas Where AI Assists in Testing (Test Maintenance - Self-Healing Tests)?
questions.answer: One of the biggest pain points in automation is maintenance. AI-assisted tools use object recognition and pattern matching to self-heal broken locators. If an element's ID or name changes, the tool adapts automatically instead of throwing an error.

questions.question: What are the concrete use-cases of AI in testing (Test case generation and augmentation)?
questions.answer:
AI can generate candidate test cases from requirements, recorded user sessions, API schemas, or historical telemetry. That speeds test coverage expansion and reduces manual scripting for common flows. Many platforms offer low-code "generate test from text/recording" features.

Benefits: faster onboarding of tests for new features; catches realistic user journeys.
Limitations: generated tests still need human review to validate intent and business logic.

questions.question: Step 4: Learn How to Test AI Systems Themselves
questions.answer:
Testing AI applications (like recommendation systems or chatbots) requires a new mindset. Focus on:

• Data Quality Testing: Ensuring training data is accurate, balanced, and representative
• Model Performance Testing: Checking precision, recall, F1-score, and bias
• Ethical Testing: Verifying fairness and explainability in model decisions
• Integration Testing: Ensuring AI components interact correctly with APIs or UIs

For hands-on learning, try testing a simple ML model using Python and libraries like:

• scikit-learn for building models
• pytest for writing tests
• pandas for data validation

questions.question: What are the industry use cases for Testing AI Systems?
questions.answer:
• Healthcare – Verifying AI diagnosis models meet accuracy standards.
• Automotive – Testing AI for autonomous vehicle decision-making.
• E-commerce – Validating AI-based product recommendation systems.

questions.question: What are the Components of an AI/ML Application to Test?
questions.answer:
A strong test strategy covers all layers:

2.1 Data Pipeline

• Data ingestion
• Cleaning
• Feature extraction
• Labeling workflows
• Storage (data lake, warehouse)

questions.question: What is the Test Strategy for AI/ML-Based Applications?
questions.answer: AI/ML-based applications behave very differently from traditional rule-based software. They evolve over time, learn from data, respond probabilistically, and often behave unpredictably in edge cases. Because of this, the test strategy for AI/ML applications must account for model accuracy, fairness, bias, data quality, safety, performance drift, interpretability, and continuous monitoring — in addition to standard functional and non-functional testing.

questions.question: What tools are used for Testing AI Systems?
questions.answer:
• TensorFlow Extended (TFX) – Model validation pipelines.
• MLflow – Experiment tracking and model lifecycle management.
• Fairlearn – Fairness and bias detection.
• Deepchecks – Automated AI model testing.
• Amazon SageMaker Clarify – Bias and explainability checks.

questions.question: What are the challenges in Testing AI Systems?
questions.answer:
• Non-deterministic Outputs: Unlike traditional software, AI outputs can vary depending on training data.
• Bias and Fairness: AI can inadvertently reflect biases present in training data.
• Model Drift: AI model accuracy may degrade over time with new/unseen data.
• Explainability: Many AI models operate as a "black box," making debugging difficult.
• Performance Scaling: AI models may require specialized infrastructure for high performance.

questions.question: What is the Nature of AI/ML Systems?
questions.answer:
Before defining a test strategy, QA engineers must understand how AI/ML systems work:

1.1 AI systems are probabilistic, not deterministic

Outputs are based on learned patterns, not fixed rules.
The same input may give slightly different results across runs (especially LLMs).

1.2 AI behavior depends heavily on data

"Bad data = bad model".
Testers must validate data quality as much as software logic.

1.3 Models evolve

Model versions change as they are retrained on new data.
Continuous testing is required to detect drift or regressions.

1.4 AI systems have unique failure modes

• Bias
• Safety risks
• Hallucinations
• Incorrect generalization
• Weaknesses to adversarial inputs

These characteristics fundamentally change how testing is planned and executed.

questions.question: What is Testing AI Systems?
questions.answer:
Testing AI Systems is the process of evaluating and validating the quality, accuracy, fairness, and reliability of AI-based applications themselves.

Here, AI is the product under test—not just a tool.
Examples include:

• Validating a machine learning model's accuracy in image recognition.
• Checking if an AI chatbot responds correctly to diverse inputs.
• Testing an AI-based fraud detection system for false positives and negatives.
• Verifying bias-free results in recommendation engines.
• Stress testing AI models for performance under large datasets.

Testing AI systems is about ensuring the AI itself works as intended, consistently, and ethically.

questions.question: What is a practical example of Testing AI Systems?
questions.answer:
Now imagine you are testing a loan approval system that uses machine learning to decide approvals based on applicant data. Your testing process would include:

• Checking if the model approves/rejects applications based on correct parameters.
• Testing for bias (e.g., ensuring decisions aren't skewed by gender or race).
• Validating that accuracy remains consistent as new data is introduced.
• Stress testing with large input datasets to check performance.

questions.question: What are the Limitations and Challenges of Codeless Automation Tools?
questions.answer:
Despite their advantages, codeless automation tools are not a silver bullet. They come with their own set of challenges:

1. Limited Flexibility
Complex test scenarios—like API chaining, database validations, or performance benchmarking—may still require custom coding, which some tools don't support well.

2. Tool Lock-In
Organizations may become dependent on a specific vendor's ecosystem. Migrating test assets to another tool can be difficult and costly.

3. Scalability Concerns
While these tools work well for small to medium projects, large enterprise-level applications with thousands of test cases may face scalability and performance issues.

4. Cost Factor
Most AI-powered codeless platforms are commercial tools with significant licensing costs, which can be prohibitive for startups or small teams.

5. Learning Curve
Though marketed as "codeless," there's still a learning curve—teams need to understand tool-specific features, AI behavior, and integration workflows.

6. Risk of Over-Reliance on AI
If AI incorrectly updates a locator or test step, it may mask defects instead of catching them, potentially leading to false positives.

questions.question: When Might Codeless Automation Tools Fall Short?
questions.answer:
• Highly Complex Workflows requiring deep logic, custom data handling, or API-database integration.
• Performance, Security, and Load Testing, which typically require specialized tools.
• Organizations with Strong Automation Teams where coding-based frameworks (like Selenium, Cypress, or Playwright) may offer greater flexibility and control.

questions.question: Are Codeless Automation Tools Worth It?
questions.answer:
The answer depends on your context:

For Agile Teams with Limited Technical Expertise: Absolutely. These tools can accelerate automation adoption and reduce maintenance headaches.

For Enterprises with Large Test Suites: Worth considering, especially for regression and UI automation. But don't expect them to replace all coded frameworks.

For Startups with Budget Constraints: Maybe not, as licensing costs could outweigh benefits compared to open-source frameworks.

For Advanced Scenarios: Still better handled with traditional coding-based frameworks.

Codeless automation tools powered by AI are not just hype—they solve real-world challenges like flaky tests, skill gaps, and slow test creation. They can significantly boost efficiency, reduce maintenance costs, and enable broader participation in test automation. But they are not a one-size-fits-all solution. Organizations should assess their specific needs, budget, team skill set, and long-term scalability goals before adopting these tools.

The best strategy may be a hybrid approach: leverage codeless AI tools for quick wins and repetitive UI tests, while using coding-based frameworks for complex, critical scenarios.
In the end, AI-powered codeless automation is worth it if adopted strategically—not blindly.

questions.question: What is the Future of Codeless AI Automation?
questions.answer:
AI will continue to make codeless automation smarter and more resilient. Future developments may include:

Predictive Test Generation using AI-driven risk analysis.
Autonomous Testing where tools create, execute, and maintain tests with minimal human input.

Deeper NLP Integration to allow stakeholders to define tests entirely in natural language.
Unified Testing Platforms combining functional, API, performance, and security testing under one AI-powered umbrella.

However, complete elimination of coding seems unlikely. Instead, hybrid models—where codeless AI tools handle simpler tests while coded frameworks manage complex scenarios—are emerging as the practical path forward.

questions.question: What are the Benefits of AI-Powered Codeless Automation?
questions.answer:
1. Faster Test Creation
With visual workflows and NLP, tests can be created in minutes instead of hours. This accelerates automation adoption even for non-technical team members.

2. Reduced Maintenance
Self-healing locators and AI-based object identification help minimize script breakage when UI elements change, a common issue in traditional automation.

3. Lower Skill Barrier
Teams without strong programming expertise can still build, execute, and manage automated tests, democratizing test automation across the organization.

4. Business-Tester Collaboration
Since test cases are written in a more understandable format, business analysts and testers can collaborate more effectively, ensuring better test coverage.

5. Smarter Test Suites
AI can help with test optimization—suggesting which test cases to run for maximum coverage or detecting redundant ones.

6. Better Integration
Modern codeless tools integrate with CI/CD pipelines, cloud testing platforms, and defect management tools, making them enterprise-ready.

questions.question: What are the Use Cases Where Codeless Automation Tools Shine?
questions.answer:
• Regression Testing: Maintaining large regression suites with AI-based self-healing reduces maintenance overhead.
• UI Testing: Visual testing, form filling, and repetitive UI actions can be automated quickly.
Business Process Testing: Domain experts can automate end-to-end workflows like order processing or loan approval.
• Smoke Testing: Rapid validation of critical functionalities in CI/CD pipelines.

questions.question: What Are Codeless Automation Tools?
questions.answer: Codeless automation tools allow testers, business users, or other non-technical stakeholders to design and execute automated test cases without writing code. Instead of scripting test steps in languages like Java, Python, or JavaScript, users interact with intuitive interfaces—such as drag-and-drop workflows, visual record-and-playback tools, or natural language processing (NLP) commands.

questions.question: How AI Powers Codeless Automation
questions.answer:
Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have supercharged these tools by:

• Self-healing tests: AI can automatically update test scripts when UI elements change (e.g., a button ID changes from btn-login to btn-signin).
• Object recognition: AI algorithms identify and interact with application elements more reliably than static locators.
• Smart suggestions: Tools can recommend test scenarios, generate test cases, or even prioritize them based on risk and usage patterns.
• Natural language automation: Some platforms let users write steps in plain English (e.g., "Click on Login button"), which the tool translates into executable actions.

Examples include Testim, Functionize, ACCELQ, Katalon, UiPath Test Suite, and even AI add-ons for Selenium-based frameworks.

questions.question: Why Are Codeless Automation Tools Becoming Popular?
questions.answer:
Several industry shifts are fueling the rise of codeless AI-powered automation:

• Shorter Release Cycles – Agile and DevOps practices demand continuous testing and fast feedback.
• Talent Gap in Automation – Not every team has skilled SDET (Software Development Engineer in Test) resources.
• Business User Involvement – Product owners and domain experts want to contribute to test automation without learning code.
• Maintenance Challenges – Traditional automation scripts often break when applications change; AI promises to reduce flakiness.
• Shift-Left Testing – Early testing in the development cycle needs rapid automation setup, which codeless tools can accelerate.

questions.answer: API: Application interface, meaning that one application is able to interact with another application in a standard way — be it over the network or locally. Web Service: a type of API, which MUST BE accessed through a network connection. Spot the difference? Yeah, the network! APIs can be exposed through local files (such as a JAR file in a Java program, .H file in C/C++ programs, etc.) to allow two local applications to communicate with each other. questions.question: What is an API?
questions.answer: API is an acronym for Application Programming Interface. API (Application Programming Interface) is a computing interface which enables communication and data exchange between two separate software systems. In software application development, API is the middle layer between the presentation (Ul) and the database layer. APIs enable communication and data exchange from one software system to another. The core functionality of the system is contained within the “business logic” layer as a series of discrete but connected business components. They are responsible for taking information from the various user interfaces (Uls), performing calculations and transactions on the database layer and then presenting the results back to the user interface.

questions.question: Why APIs?
questions.answer: The importance of APIs is that it lets different organizations create software applications that rely on other application and services without having to constantly update their application when the internals of the dependent applications or services change. As long as the API itself remains stable, the internal implementation can change. This is an important feature of APIs, they consist of a part that doesn’t change — “the interface or contract” that specifies the operations, data formats and behaviours and the implementation that can change as needed.

questions.answer: Endpoint: the URI + path/query parameters to send the request to. Request-type: different HTTP methods. Request: the payload in xml/json/etc. format. Auth: check for authorization and permission. Response: response from the server.

Authentication: verifying the auth mechanism [happy-flow/time-out/invalid/etc.] HTTP methods: which all methods are supported. HTTP Status Code: Basic check before validating the response. Error conditions: how well the API handles the invalid inputs. Performance & Security aspects.

questions.question: What is API Testing?
questions.answer: API testing is a practice that tests the APIs directly — from their functionality, reliability, performance, to security. There are three separate layers in a typical app: the presentation (or user interface) layer, the business layer, and the database layer for Modeling and manipulating data. API testing is performed at the most critical layer: business, in which business logic processing is carried out and all transactions between the user interface and database layers happen. While there are many aspects of API testing, it generally consists of making requests to a single or sometimes multiple API endpoints and validate the response - whether for performance, security, functional correctness, or just a status check. API testing is used to determine whether APIs return the correct response (in the expected format) for a broad range of feasible requests, react properly to edge cases such as failures and unexpected/extreme inputs, deliver responses in an acceptable amount of time, and respond securely to potential security attacks. API testing flow is quite simple with three main steps: e Send the request with necessary input data. e Get the response having output data. e Verify that the response returned as expected in the requirement.

questions.question: What are HTTP Status Codes?
questions.answer:
HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers returned by web servers to indicate the outcome of an HTTP request. Each code is categorized into five classes, defined by the first digit, which indicates the general response type:

1. 1xx (Informational): Indicates that the request has been received and is being processed.
2. 2xx (Success): Indicates that the request was successfully received, understood, and accepted.
3. 3xx (Redirection): Indicates that further action needs to be taken by the client to fulfill the request.
4. 4xx (Client Error): Indicates that there was an error with the client's request.
5. 5xx (Server Error): Indicates that the server failed to fulfill a valid request.

Let’s explore these categories in detail.

1xx: Informational Responses

The 1xx category contains codes that convey information about the request’s progress. Though less common, they are important for understanding the status of long-running requests.
• 100 Continue: This code indicates that the initial part of the request has been received and that the client should continue sending the rest of the request.
• 101 Switching Protocols: Used when the client and server agree to switch protocols (e.g., from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2).

2xx: Successful Responses

The 2xx status codes indicate that a request was successfully processed.
• 200 OK: This is the standard response for a successful HTTP request. It indicates that the server successfully processed the request and returned the requested resource.
• 201 Created: This code signifies that the request has been fulfilled, and a new resource has been created. This is commonly used in POST requests.
• 204 No Content: Indicates that the server successfully processed the request, but there is no content to return (often used for DELETE requests).

3xx: Redirection

Redirection codes inform the client that further action is required to complete the request.
• 301 Moved Permanently: This status code indicates that the requested resource has been permanently moved to a new URL. Clients should update their bookmarks and links.
• 302 Found: This code indicates that the resource is temporarily located at a different URI, but future requests should still use the original URI.
• 304 Not Modified: Indicates that the resource has not been modified since the last request. This helps with caching and reduces unnecessary data transfer.

4xx: Client Errors

The 4xx category indicates that there was an error with the client’s request, which means the issue lies on the client-side.
• 400 Bad Request: This code signifies that the server cannot process the request due to a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax).
• 401 Unauthorized: Indicates that authentication is required to access the requested resource. The client must provide valid credentials.
• 403 Forbidden: This code means that the server understood the request, but refuses to authorize it. This could be due to insufficient permissions.
• 404 Not Found: One of the most well-known status codes, this indicates that the requested resource could not be found on the server.

5xx: Server Errors

The 5xx status codes indicate that the server failed to fulfill a valid request due to an error on its side.
• 500 Internal Server Error: A generic error message indicating that an unexpected condition was encountered. This means the server is encountering problems that prevent it from fulfilling the request.
• 502 Bad Gateway: This code indicates that a server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, received an invalid response from the upstream server.
• 503 Service Unavailable: This status code means that the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, usually due to maintenance or overload.

The Importance of HTTP Status Codes

1. Debugging and Troubleshooting: When a web application experiences issues, status codes provide insights into what went wrong, helping developers identify and fix errors efficiently.
2. User Experience: By providing clear feedback through status codes, developers can enhance the user experience. For example, a well-implemented 404 page can guide users back to functioning parts of the site.
3. Search Engine Optimization (SEO): Search engines use status codes to determine the indexability of web pages. Properly managing 301 and 404 codes, for instance, can significantly impact a website's SEO performance.
4. API Interactions: In RESTful APIs, status codes are vital for conveying the outcome of API requests, allowing clients to handle responses accordingly.

HTTP status codes are a fundamental part of web communication, serving as a bridge between clients and servers. They convey essential information about the outcome of requests, helping both developers and users navigate the complex landscape of the internet. By understanding these codes and their meanings, developers can build more robust web applications, troubleshoot issues more effectively, and enhance overall user experience. As the web continues to evolve, mastery of HTTP status codes will remain a vital skill for anyone involved in web development or online services.

questions.question: What are the components of an API Request?
questions.answer:
An API (Application Programming Interface) request is the way clients (like browsers, mobile apps, or automated scripts) communicate with servers to exchange data. When you make an API request, you’re essentially asking the server to perform an action — such as fetching data, adding a record, updating information, or deleting something.

Every API request consists of several key components that define what the client wants and how the server should respond. Let’s go through each component in detail:

1. Endpoint (or URL)

The endpoint is the address of the resource you’re trying to access. It tells the API which specific resource you want to interact with.

• Example: https://api.github.com/users/kanchankapoor/repos

Here:

• https:// → the protocol (communication method)
• api.github.com → the base URL (domain of the API)
• /users/kanchankapoor/repos → the endpoint path that specifies which data you want (repositories of a user)

Think of an endpoint as the exact “door” to the data you want.

2. HTTP Method (or Verb)

The HTTP method defines what action you want to perform on the resource. The most common methods are:



For example, sending a GET request to /users might return a list of users, while a POST request to /users might add a new user.

3. Headers

Headers are key-value pairs that carry metadata about the request. They provide information about authentication, content type, accepted response format, etc.
Common HTTP headers include:

• Content-Type: Defines the format of the request body (e.g., application/json, application/xml)
• Accept: Specifies what format the client expects in the response
• Authorization: Used for authentication (e.g., Bearer <token>)
• User-Agent: Identifies the client application making the request

Example:

Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer 123abc456xyz

Headers are like the “envelope” of your request — they carry instructions and credentials.

4. Request Body (or Payload)

The request body contains the actual data you’re sending to the server, usually in POST, PUT, or PATCH requests.

For example, if you want to create a new user:

{
  "name": "Kanchan Kapoor",
  "role": "QA Engineer",
  "email": "kanchan@example.com"
}

The server reads this data and creates a new record based on it.

GET and DELETE requests typically don’t have a body since they’re fetching or removing data.

5. Query Parameters

Query parameters are additional key-value pairs appended to the URL to filter, sort, or customize the data you want to retrieve.

They appear after a ? in the URL and are separated by &.

Example: https://api.example.com/users?role=QA&status=active

This tells the API to return only users who are QA and active.

Query parameters fine-tune what data you get back, similar to search filters.

6. Path Parameters

Path parameters are variables embedded directly in the URL path to specify a particular resource.

Example: https://api.example.com/users/123

Here, 123 is the user ID, used to fetch or manipulate that specific user’s data.

If query parameters are filters, path parameters are direct references to a single item.

7. Authentication / Authorization

Most APIs are protected, meaning the client must prove its identity before accessing data.
Common authentication methods include:

• API Key (e.g., ?api_key=abc123)
• Bearer Token (in header)
• OAuth 2.0 tokens
• Basic Auth (username + password)

Example:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6...

Without proper authorization, your request will be rejected (often with a 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden response).

8. Optional: Cookies or Session Data

In some APIs (especially web-based ones), the server might rely on cookies or session tokens to maintain authentication or track user activity between requests.

Putting It All Together

Here’s a complete example of an API request in action:

Example: Create a new user
POST /users HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer 123abc456xyz
{
  "name": "Kanchan Kapoor",
  "email": "kanchan@example.com",
  "role": "QA Engineer"
}

Here:
• POST → HTTP method
• /users → endpoint
• Content-Type + Authorization → headers
• JSON block → request body

Summary Table


In Summary

An API request is a structured communication from a client to a server, consisting of:

• A URL (endpoint) to identify the resource
• An HTTP method to specify the action
• Optional headers, query/path parameters, and body for details
• And often authentication to secure access

Together, these components ensure that the client and server can communicate efficiently, securely, and meaningfully.

questions.question: What are Epics, User Stories, and Tasks?
questions.answer:
Epic: a big story that will help the end-user to resolve a business problem.

User Story: smaller pieces of functionality, and they directly map to an epic. A narrative text(s) that describe an interaction of the user and the system, focusing on the value a user gains from the system.

Format: As a < user > I want to < goal > so that < acceptance criteria >

Note: Scrum doesn't say that the requirements need to be in the story format. As per Scrum, you can have the requirements in any form, though the story is the most popular format to document requirements.

Tasks: actual work that needs to be done to complete a story. A Story is divided into tasks, and once all these tasks finish, we can mark the story as "Done" or "Completed." E.g., create a UI form, develop API, create a backend database table, etc.

questions.question: What are Agile principles 10-12?
questions.answer:
10. Simplicity--the art of maximizing the amount of work not done--is essential.
11. The best architectures, requirements, and designs emerge from self-organizing teams.
12. At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behaviour accordingly.

questions.question: What is the difference between Waterfall and Agile?
questions.answer:
Waterfall is essentially making a good plan and sticking to it, while Agile utilises a more flexible, iterative approach. Waterfall is more sequential and pre-defined, while Agile is more adaptable as a project progresses.

- Agile is an incremental and iterative approach; Waterfall is a linear and sequential approach.
- Agile separates a project into sprints; Waterfall divides a project into phases.
- Agile introduces a product mindset with a focus on customer satisfaction; Waterfall focuses on successful project delivery.
- Agile allows requirement changes at any time; Waterfall avoids scope changes once the project starts.
- Testing is performed concurrently with development in Agile; testing phase comes only after the build phase in a Waterfall project.
- Agile enables the project team to operate without a dedicated project manager; Waterfall requires a project manager who plays an essential role in every phase.

questions.question: What is Extreme Programming (XP)?
questions.answer:
An agile software development framework that is the most specific regarding appropriate engineering practices for software development.

- Dynamically changing software requirements
- Risks caused by fixed time projects using new technology
- Small, co-located extended development team
- The technology you are using allows for automated unit and functional tests

The core of XP is the interconnected set of software development practices listed below:
- The Planning Game, Small Releases, Metaphor, Simple Design, Testing, Refactoring
- Pair Programming: all production software is developed by two people sitting at the same machine.
- Collective Ownership
- Continuous Integration: a practice where code changes are immediately tested when they are added to a larger code base.
- 40-hour week, On-site Customer, Coding Standard

questions.question: What is a Burnup chart?
questions.answer:
A burn up chart shows how much work has been completed, and the total amount of work. There are two main lines shown on the chart: one for the total project work planned, and the other for tracking the work completed to date.

By comparing the work, a team has accomplished so far with the total amount of work planned, it allows project managers and teams to quickly see how their workload is progressing and whether project completion is on schedule.

questions.question: Explain the Agile value: Responding to change over following a plan.
questions.answer: Start with a plan that gives us enough idea of the direction we want to move. Then as we proceed and seeing new events unfolding in front of us, we incorporate those realities into the ongoing work.

questions.question: What is Kanban?
questions.answer:
Kanban is a popular framework used to implement agile. Work items are represented visually on a Kanban board, allowing team members to see the state of every piece of work at any time.

For example, you might create lists for "Backlog," "Up Next," "In Progress," and "Done!" Each task is organized as a card, which you move across the lists as they are queued up, worked on, and completed.

questions.question: What is a Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal?
questions.answer:
The list of all items from the product backlog that need to be worked on during a sprint. A real-time picture of the work that the team currently plans to complete during the sprint.
- It is the outcome of sprint planning meeting sessions
- The development team owns the sprint backlog and divides tasks according to their skills
- It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Development Team plans to accomplish
- The sprint backlog is dynamic in nature because each sprint has repeated changes to reach the goal.

questions.question: What are Story Points?
questions.answer:
Traditional software teams give estimates in a time format: days, weeks, months. Many agile teams, however, have transitioned to story points. Story points are units of measure for expressing an estimate of the overall effort required to fully implement a product backlog item or any other piece of work. Teams assign story points relative to work complexity, the amount of work, and risk or uncertainty.

Note: Story points go wrong when they're used to judge people, assign detailed timelines and resources, and when they're mistaken for a measure of productivity. Instead, teams should use story points to understand the size of the work and the prioritization of the work.

questions.question: What are the benefits of agility?
questions.answer:
Stakeholder engagement: Stakeholders and team members have opportunities to observe and test throughout the project which allows for adjustments and changes to be made as things move forward. This greater "user focus" means that on delivery it's likely the outcome will be more in line with expectations - even if they have evolved along the way.

Focuses on Business Value: By allowing the client to determine the priority of features, the team understands what's most important to the client's business, and can deliver the features that provide the most business value.

Allows for Change: While the team needs to stay focused on delivering an agreed-to subset of the product's features during each iteration, there is an opportunity to constantly refine and reprioritize the overall product backlog. New or changed backlog items can be planned for the next iteration, providing the opportunity to introduce changes within a few weeks.

Collaboration: Agile encourages teamwork, collaboration, self-organisation and accountability. This helps with overall motivation and commitment to a project's outcomes and goals.

Customer satisfaction: Customer-focused approach, resulting in increased customer satisfaction.

Early and Predictable Delivery: By using time-boxed, fixed schedule iterations, new features are delivered quickly and frequently, with a high level of predictability. If time to market for a specific application is a greater concern than releasing a full feature set at initial launch, Agile can more quickly produce a basic version of working software which can be built upon in successive iterations.

questions.question: What are the first three Agile principles?
questions.answer:
1. Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.
2. Welcome changing requirements, even late in development. Agile processes harness change for the customer's competitive advantage.
3. Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale.

questions.question: What is the Definition of Done (DoD)?
questions.answer:
Usually, a checklist of all the work that team needs to do before the team can call the user story/product increment as "Done".

The Definition of Done (DoD) must be clear to all the stakeholders. It ensures that when the Scrum team calls out a product increment as "Done", everyone has the same shared understanding of what this means. Example:
- Code is written.
- Code is documented.
- Code review has been completed.
- Unit test passed
- Build has been made and deployed on a testing environment.
- Acceptance criteria for each issue met
- Functional tests passed
- Non-functional requirements met
- Test automation scripts are developed & executed
- Product owner accepts the User Story

Note: Scrum team defines the definition of done. They are the ones who will be accountable to meet this definition, so it's essential that the team creates it and agrees to it.

questions.question: What is the difference between Release and Sprint?
questions.answer:
The heart of Scrum is a Sprint, a time-box of one week or one month during which a potentially releasable product increment (feature or set of features within a product) is created. Release, on the other hand, is the complete feature set for that particular version of the product.

Both are considered "shippable" and able to be consumed by the end user, but generally speaking the output of a Sprint is just the short-term part of the end product and cannot stand alone while the output of a Release is the long term, strategic product itself.

questions.question: Explain the Agile value: Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.
questions.answer: When software is developed based on a pre-defined contract (without constant feedback), the result is often a product that does not completely satisfy the customers' needs. That is why Agile emphasizes to take constant feedback from the customer throughout the development process.

questions.question: Explain the Agile value: Working software over comprehensive documentation.
questions.answer: Instead of wasting a lot of time creating lengthy documents and then taking feedback based on those documents, we should take the feedback based on working software.

questions.question: What are Agile principles 4-6?
questions.answer:
4. Business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project.
5. Build projects around motivated individuals. Give them the environment and support they need, and trust them to get the job done.
6. The most efficient and effective method of conveying information to and within a development team is face-to-face conversation.

questions.question: What is Agile Testing?
questions.answer:
A testing practice that follows the rules and principles of agile. Unlike Waterfall method, Agile testing can begin at the start of the project with continuous integration.

Agile Testing is not sequential like Waterfall but continuous, i.e., testing happens in parallel with feature development as part of every sprint - goes hand in hand with development work and provides an ongoing feedback loop into the quality.

It is a collaborative effort between testers, developers, product owners and even customers.

questions.question: What is the Bucket System estimation technique?
questions.answer: Using the same sequence as Planning Poker, a group or a team estimate items by placing them in "buckets". The Bucket System is a much faster because there is a "divide-and-conquer" phase.

questions.question: What is agile?
questions.answer:
"A group of software development methodologies based on 'iterative' development, where requirements and solutions evolve through collaboration between self-organizing cross-functional teams".

- Group of methodologies: there's no one right way to implement agile. There are many different types of methodologies from which to choose — Kanban, Scrum, Extreme Programming (XP), Feature-driven development (FDD), Dynamic Systems Development Method (DSDM), Crystal, Lean.
- Iterative development: a 'repeated' interval in which work items are fully developed and tested.
- Collaboration: connect the right people from different groups to work together on tasks, boosting cross-team collaboration and productivity.
- self-organizing cross-functional teams: As the name says, the team is able to craft their way of working (self-organizing) and is a mix of people who have access to all the skills necessary to effectively deliver value to customers (cross-functional).

'Agile' represents the adaptiveness and response to change, delivering business value through product 'increments' - at regular intervals. A mindset informed by the Agile Manifesto's values and principles.

questions.question: What is Scrum?
questions.answer:
Scrum is a subset of Agile. It is a lightweight process framework for agile development, and the most widely-used one.

- Process framework: a particular set of practices that must be followed. For example, Scrum process is distinguished by specific concepts and practices - Roles, Artifacts, and Time Boxes.
- Lightweight: overhead of the process is kept as small as possible, to maximize the amount of productive time available for getting useful work done.

questions.question: What is Scrumban?
questions.answer: Project management framework that combines important features of two popular agile methodologies: Scrum and Kanban. Scrumban merges the structure and predictability of Scrum with Kanban's flexibility and continuous workflow. It embraces on-demand planning. It involves applying Kanban principles - visualization of workflow, and flexible processes—to a team's Scrum framework. Scrumban teams also use Kanban processes, such as the pull system, which provides a continuous workflow. That is, tasks are pulled into the doing column when the team is ready to execute.

questions.question: What is Sprint Planning?
questions.answer:
What needs to be delivered in the current Sprint iteration? Every Sprint begins with Sprint planning when the entire team gets together to agree on what needs to deliver in the Sprint (Sprint Goals). The entire team clearly defines deliverables for the Sprint and assigns the work necessary to achieve that goal. Entire scrum team takes part in Sprint Planning to understand the work or tasks to be performed in that Sprint and create a sprint goal.

Note: Sprint planning is timeboxed, maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint.

Sprint Goal: Each Sprint needs to have a potentially releasable deliverable. How do we achieve that? By having a clearly defined Sprint goal. The basis of the Sprint goal is the essential features of the product that needs to be built first.

questions.question: What is SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework)?
questions.answer: Scaled agile framework (SAFe) - a set of organizational patterns to guide enterprises in scaling lean and agile practices beyond a single team. i.e., if you want to implement standard agile practices across projects & teams within an organization.

questions.question: What is a Burndown chart?
questions.answer:
A burn down chart shows how much work is remaining to be done in the project. Its purpose is to enable that the project is on the track to deliver the expected solution within the desired schedule.

A graphical representation of work left to do versus time. You can define remaining work based on Stories or Tasks. The ideal line is going down in a straight line from top left to down right. This indicates a healthy project and a well-functioning Scrum team. Value is being delivered constantly in a linear fashion.

questions.question: What is the Big/Uncertain/Small estimation technique?
questions.answer: For super-fast Agile estimation, the items to be estimated are simply placed by the group in one of three categories: big, uncertain and small. The group starts by discussing a few together, and then, like the Bucket System, uses divide-and-conquer to go through the rest of the items.

questions.question: What is Planning Poker?
questions.answer:
Planning poker makes use of story points to estimate the difficulty of the task at hand. Based on the Fibonacci sequence, the story point values that can be assigned are 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40 and 100. Each of these represent a different level of complexity.

When the discussions around user story are finished, team members will select a card with the story point they believe needs to be assigned to the user story. Further discussions will ensue until there is a consensus.

questions.question: What is a Sprint Retrospective?
questions.answer: The team discusses what went right, what went wrong, and how to improve. They decide on how to fix the problems and create a plan for improvements to be enacted during the next sprint. Regardless of how good a Scrum team is, there is always room for improvement.

questions.question: What is a Zero Sprint?
questions.answer:
A Sprint 0 is the name often given to a short effort to create a vision and a rough product backlog which allows creating an estimation of a product release. Why? Since there are things that need to be done before a Scrum project can start.

Note: From official scrum guide - there is no Sprint 0. In practical world, when a team sets out to adopt Scrum - usually Sprint 0 is used for the first time to adopt the scrum framework in the current business process.

questions.question: What is the Daily Scrum/Stand Up?
questions.answer:
Also known as daily stand-up, it is a 15-minute daily meeting where the team has a chance to get on the same page and put together a strategy for the next 24 hours. The agenda being,
- What was done yesterday
- What will be done today
- Are there any impediments that are preventing the team from meeting the sprint goal?

questions.question: What is Velocity in Agile?
questions.answer:
Agile Velocity is an extremely simple method for measuring the rate at which scrum teams consistently deliver business value. In other words - How much product backlog effort a team can handle in one sprint? It's the rate at which a team delivers stories from the product backlog, i.e., sum of estimates of delivered (i.e., accepted) features per iteration. It can be measured in story points, days, ideal days, or hours that the Scrum team delivers — all of which are considered acceptable.

A team delivers 20 and 30 story points in the first & second iteration respectively. The average velocity = Sum of Story points delivered / Number of iterations = (20 + 30)/2 = 25 Story points!

- Only the aggregate velocity of the team matters, and the phrase "individual velocity" is meaningless.
- Velocity is NOT productivity. Instead of a speedometer, it is more like a measurement of a team's rhythm and should be used to monitor team health.

The goal is not maximized velocity, but rather optimal velocity over time, which takes into account many factors including the quality of the end product. Benefits:
- Reporting, i.e., how much value is delivered (Story points/User stories)
- Resource and project planning (timelines)
- Adjusting project scope and business priorities, and forecasting release dates
- Identifying and removing obstacles that affect velocity

Do not try to over-complicate velocity — it really is a straight forward concept and a great deal of its value lies in its inherent simplicity.

questions.question: Explain the Agile value: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
questions.answer: We should focus more on having competent people working together effectively. Processes and tools are not harmful but don't use them until they make things easy and effective.

questions.question: What makes a good user story? (INVEST)
questions.answer:
The acronym INVEST helps to remember a widely accepted set of criteria, or checklist, to assess the quality of a user story.

A good user story should be:
- "I" ndependent (of all others)
- "N" egotiable (not a specific contract for features)
- "V" aluable (or vertical)
- "E" stimable (to a good approximation)
- "S" mall (so as to fit within an iteration)
- "T" estable (in principle, even if there isn't a test for it yet)

Each user story is expected to yield, once implemented, a contribution to the value of the overall product, irrespective of the order of implementation; these and other assumptions are captured by the INVEST formula.

questions.question: What is a Product Backlog?
questions.answer:
It's a document that acts as a single source of requirements for everything needed in the product. It includes new features, changes to existing features, bug fixes, infrastructure setups, etc. It is constantly evolving and is never complete. The Product Owner manages the Product Backlog, including how it's made available to the scrum team, its content, and how it's ordered and prioritized, everything. The Product Owner and the rest of the scrum team work together to review the Product Backlog and make adjustments as and when necessary.

Each requirement in the product backlog have a,
- Description
- Order based on priority
- Estimate
- Value to the business

questions.question: What is Test-Driven Development (TDD)?
questions.answer:
A software development process that relies on the repetition of a very short development cycle: requirements are turned into very specific test cases, then the software is improved to pass the new tests, only.

Each iteration starts with a set of tests written for a new piece of functionality. These tests are supposed to fail during the start of iteration as there will be no application code corresponding to the tests. In the next phase of the iteration Application code is written with an intention to pass all the tests written earlier in the iteration. Once the application code is ready tests are run.

Any failures in the test run are marked and more Application code is written/re-factored to make these tests pass. Once application code is added/re-factored the tests are run again. This cycle keeps on happening till all the tests pass. Once all the tests pass, we can be sure that all the features for which tests were written have been developed.

questions.question: What is the Testing Pyramid?
questions.answer:
The "Test Pyramid" is a metaphor that tells us to group software tests into buckets of different granularity. It also gives an idea of how many tests we should have in each of these groups.

The assumption here is that automated unit tests are cheap, easy, fast to run and isolated, compared to those slow, brittle, hard to write end-to-end tests that require a full working system and a web browser or mobile device. The foundation of a test effort should be unit tests, with fewer service tests and very few end-to-end tests, creating a bit of a pyramid.

questions.question: What are Acceptance Criteria?
questions.answer:
Acceptance Criteria are a set of statements, each with a clear pass/fail result, that specify both functional and non-functional requirements, and are applicable at the Epic, Feature, and Story Level. Acceptance criteria constitute our "Definition of Done", i.e., when a work item is complete and working as expected. The Given/When/Then format is helpful way to specify criteria:

Given some precondition When I do some action Then I expect some result.

In simple terms, acceptance criteria refer to a set of predefined requirements that must be met to mark a user story complete. It clearly defines the scope, desired outcomes of, and testing criteria for pieces of functionality that the delivery team is working on.

Note: Often Acceptance Criteria are defined by the Product Owner (PO) when creating a Product Backlog Item and then adapted and extended in the Backlog Refinement.

questions.question: What is a Sprint?
questions.answer:
Sprint is a short, time-boxed iteration to allow the scrum team to focus on delivering value to the customer. During a sprint, the team works to create a done, usable, and potentially releasable product increment. Example, a 2-weeks sprint where a scrum team completes 4 user stories, i.e., ready for review at sprint end.

Timeboxing simply means to limit the maximum time an activity can take. It's the core concept of a Scrum model. Typically, a Sprint duration is 1, 2, 3, or 4 weeks, and this varies from organization to organization. Within this timebox, the Scrum team has to finish the agreed set of work.

questions.question: What is a Sprint Review?
questions.answer:
Held at the end of each sprint, the team presents completed work to product owner and stakeholders for approval or any feedback that they might have. Usually, the Product Owner starts by talking about the goals of the Sprint and what functionality is delivered. The Scrum Master can show burn-down charts and the velocity of the team. After which the development team will showcase their work.

Note: Sprint review is timeboxed. The duration is a maximum of 1 hour for every week of Sprint duration.

questions.question: What is the Ordering Protocol estimation technique?
questions.answer: Items are placed in a random order on a scale labelled simply "low" to "high". Each person participating takes turns making a "move". A move involves one of the following actions: change the position of an item by one spot lower or one spot higher, talking about an item, or passing. If everyone passes, the ordering is done.

questions.question: What are the four values of the Agile Manifesto?
questions.answer:
The Agile Manifesto values are:
* Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
* Working software over comprehensive documentation
* Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
* Responding to change over following a plan

That is, while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.

questions.question: What are Agile principles 7-9?
questions.answer:
7. Working software is the primary measure of progress.
8. Agile processes promote sustainable development. The sponsors, developers, and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.
9. Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility.

questions.question: What is Scrum of Scrums?
questions.answer:
"Scrum of Scrums" is a scaled agile technique that offers a way to connect multiple scrum teams. Think of it as multiple smaller scrum teams who are coordinating to deliver a complex product. The key here is to enable effective & efficient coordination between smaller scrum teams to deliver full value.

A cross-team synchronization method used in case when multiple teams are involved, to support the agile teams in collaborating and coordinating their work with other teams. This involves conducting a scrum meeting of reps from individual scrum teams, additional roles like Chief product owner, SOS master, etc.

questions.question: What are the Scrum roles?
questions.answer:
There are three distinct roles defined in Scrum - ScrumMaster, the Product Owner, and the Team.

Scrum master, the keeper of the process:
- Responsible for making the process run smoothly. Make sure that the goals and scope of the project are understood by everyone involved
- Remove impediments & obstacles that could impact team's productivity.
- Organizing and facilitating the critical meetings.
- Keep information about the Team's progress up to date and visible to all parties.
- Guide the team and product owner to improve the effectiveness of their practices.
- Makes changes to increase the productivity of the scrum team.

Product owner, the keeper of the requirements:
- 'Single source of truth' for the team regarding requirements
- Prioritizing the requirements.
- interface between the business (the customers) and the team.
- Managing the product backlog & making sure that it is visible, transparent, and clear.
- Progressing the value of the work done and making rational decisions.
- Collaborating with the development team and stakeholders.

Agile team:
- Self-organizing: Team members decide how to break work into tasks, and how to allocate tasks to individuals, throughout the Sprint.
- Cross-functional: a group of people with different functional expertise working toward a common goal.
- Plan the sprint with guidelines from the product owner and scrum master
- Perform sprint execution and adapt the sprint according to changing user requirements. Do the hands-on work of developing and testing the product.
- Help product owner groom the product backlog.
- Inspect and adapt the product & process.

questions.question: What is a Product Increment?
questions.answer:
"What gets produced at the end of a development period or timebox".

The most important artifact is the product increment, or in other words, the sum of product work completed during a Sprint, combined with all work completed during previous sprints. In a Scrum environment, the team would have a 'definition of done', so that they know that the product increment is complete.

questions.question: What is Agile Estimation?
questions.answer:
Agile estimation is about evaluating the effort required to complete each work item listed in the prioritized backlog, which, in turn, helps in better sprint planning. Most Agile estimation techniques use relative units. This means that we don't try to estimate dollars or days directly. Instead, we use "points" or even qualitative labels and simply compare the items we are estimating to each other.

Agile estimations are essential for:
- Making teams accountable for deliverables
- Inducing discipline across the Agile team
- Predicting the approximate time, it will take to finish a project
- Enabling better sprint management
- Improving team productivity

Note: Estimation is done by the entire team during Sprint Planning Meeting. The objective of the estimation would be to consider the User Stories for the sprint by priority and by the ability of the team to deliver during the time box of the sprint.

questions.question: What is the difference between Iteration and Increment?
questions.answer:
Iteration: a 'repeated' interval (typically 1-4 weeks) in which work items are fully developed and tested. Projects are made up of as many iterations as needed.

Increment: Product increment, i.e., what gets produced at the end of a development period or timebox.

questions.question: What is T-Shirt Sizes estimation?
questions.answer: Items are categorized into t-shirt sizes: XS, S, M, L, XL. The sizes can, if needed, be given numerical values after the estimation is done. This is a very informal technique, and can be used quickly with a large number of items.

questions.question: What are the three Scrum artifacts?
questions.answer: The three Scrum artifacts are: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Product Increment.

Short sprints and constant feedback - easier to cope with the changes or course corrections.

questions.question: What is difference between Epic, User stories & Tasks?
questions.answer:
Epic - something so big it probably won't fit into a sprint and should be broken down into stories. T-shirt sizing is a common way to size epics. Epics are usually defined during initial product roadmap and decomposed into stories in the product backlog as more is learned.

Story - something actionable and small enough to fit in a sprint. These are story pointed and defined using INVEST criteria. Stories should deliver a vertical slice of functionality to the customer that is valuable and complete by the end of an iteration.

Tasks - decomposed parts of a story that get into HOW the story will be completed. Tasks can be hour estimated if desired. Tasks are usually defined by the people doing the work (developers, QA, etc), whereas stories and epics are generally created by the customer or the product owner representing the customer.

questions.question: Positive & Negative about Waterfall & Agile
questions.answer:
Waterfall is disciplined by design and well documented. Suitable for projects where there are many interfaces and dependencies. It is easy to estimate costs, create timelines, and stick to deadlines. Since it is more plan-oriented, it is more secure and builds confidence of what will finally be delivered. Additionally, it has an easy learning curve to start working on a project ©

The biggest catch - Client won't see a working product until late in the life cycle which means assurance of products being fit-for-purpose is demonstrated very late. Defining requirements in early stage is not easy and it’s costly to make changes in later phases.

The Iterative design process of Agile gives it the flexibility to pivot when needed and reduces risk by constant user feedback during development. It is apt for projects where the end-goals are not clearly defined. Development/Testing is often more user-focused and reporting is effective via visual charts/Kanban/etc.

Agile is simple to understand in principle but hard to do well in practice. It requires high levels of collaboration and very regular communication between users. It’s challenging on large projects or where co-location is not possible. Not that strong when dealing with lead times and major dependencies. It is hard to predict timelines or budgets. It is an inherent tendency to neglect documentation.

Agile and Waterfall are very different. Neither of it is inherently better than the other. You just need to understand which method is better suited to your project needs.
