questions.question: What are different levels of Software Testing?
questions.answer:
The different levels of software testing represent the various stages at which software is tested during the development lifecycle. Each level focuses on a specific aspect of the system — from verifying small units of code to validating the complete application against business needs.

These levels ensure that software is tested systematically, with defects being detected as early as possible, thereby reducing costs and improving quality.

1. Unit Testing (Component or Module Testing)

Purpose: To verify that individual components or small pieces of code (like functions, methods, or classes) work as expected in isolation.

Performed By: Developers, usually during the coding phase.

Focus: Testing the internal logic of each code unit.

Example:

• Testing a login() function to check if it correctly validates user credentials.
• Verifying if a calculateTotal() method returns the correct output.

Tools Commonly Used:

• JUnit, TestNG (for Java)
• PyTest, unittest (for Python)
• NUnit (for .NET)

Benefits:

• Early detection of coding bugs
• Easier debugging (since tests focus on small code units)
• Ensures code stability before integration

Think of unit testing as checking every “brick” before building the house.

2. Integration Testing

Purpose: To ensure that different modules or services work together correctly when integrated. Even if individual modules work fine, their interaction may cause unexpected issues.

Performed By: Developers or testers, after unit testing is complete.

Focus: Verifying the data flow and interface compatibility between modules or components.

Example:

• Testing whether the Login module interacts properly with the Database module.
• Checking if data from the frontend correctly reaches the backend API.

Types of Integration Testing Approaches:

• Big Bang: All modules integrated at once and tested together.
• Incremental: Modules are integrated and tested step by step (Top-down, Bottom-up, or Sandwich approach).

Tools Commonly Used:

• Postman, REST Assured (for API integrations)
• JUnit, TestNG (with integration test suites)

Benefits:

• Detects interface issues early
• Ensures data consistency across modules
• Verifies that the system behaves as a cohesive unit

If unit testing checks the bricks, integration testing checks the mortar between them.

3. System Testing

Purpose: To validate the complete and fully integrated application against the functional and non-functional requirements. This is the first level of testing where the entire system is tested as a whole.

Performed By: A dedicated testing team (QA engineers) in a controlled test environment.

Focus: Verifying that the entire system meets both functional (features) and non-functional (performance, security, usability) requirements.

Example:

• Testing if the end-to-end user registration process works correctly.
• Verifying if the system handles concurrent users without performance degradation.
• Checking security, compatibility, and installation behavior.

Types of Testing Performed at System Level:

• Functional Testing
• Usability Testing
• Performance Testing
• Security Testing
• Regression Testing

Tools Commonly Used:

• Selenium, Cypress, Playwright (functional)
• JMeter, LoadRunner (performance)
• OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite (security)

Benefits:

• Confirms that the system behaves as expected in real scenarios
• Validates both visible and hidden functionalities
• Builds confidence for final release

System testing is like testing the entire car — not just its parts.

4. Acceptance Testing (User Acceptance Testing – UAT)

Purpose: To verify that the software meets business requirements and is ready for deployment. This is the final testing level before the product is released to production.

Performed By: End-users, clients, or business representatives, sometimes with support from QA.

Focus: Ensuring that the product satisfies real-world usage and business goals.

Example:

• A client verifies that the new billing system correctly calculates invoices as per company policy.
• A user checks if the workflow of an HR application matches their daily process.

Types of Acceptance Testing:

• User Acceptance Testing (UAT): Performed by end users.
• Operational Acceptance Testing (OAT): Focuses on operational readiness (backup, recovery, monitoring).
• Contract and Regulation Testing: Ensures compliance with legal or contractual requirements.

Benefits:

• Confirms the system is production-ready
• Minimizes post-deployment issues
• Ensures user satisfaction

Acceptance testing is like the final test drive before handing over the car to the customer.

Summary Table


Why These Levels Matter

Each level of software testing serves a unique purpose in catching defects early and ensuring quality:

1. Unit Testing → Detects early coding issues
2. Integration Testing → Finds interface and communication errors
3. System Testing → Ensures end-to-end functionality
4. Acceptance Testing → Confirms business value and user satisfaction

Together, these levels create a layered defense against software defects — improving reliability, performance, and user trust.

In Summary

The different levels of software testing — Unit, Integration, System, and Acceptance — form a structured approach to verifying software quality from the ground up. Each level builds upon the previous one, ensuring that software is tested thoroughly — from individual components to real-world usage.

This systematic approach ensures that the final product is stable, functional, and meets the user’s expectations, paving the way for a smooth and successful release.

questions.question: What are different types of Software Testing?
questions.answer:
Software testing is a critical process in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) that ensures the product meets its requirements, functions correctly, and provides a high-quality user experience. Testing verifies and validates the software against both functional and non-functional requirements.

Testing can be categorized in several ways—based on purpose, technique, level, and approach. Let’s explore these categories in detail.

1. Based on Functionality

This is the most common classification of software testing, divided into Functional and Non-Functional testing.

A. Functional Testing

Functional testing focuses on validating the software against the business or user requirements. It ensures that each feature works as intended.

Common Types of Functional Testing:

1. Unit Testing: Tests individual components or functions of the code in isolation.
Example: Verifying a login method returns the correct response when given valid credentials.
2. Integration Testing: Ensures that different modules or services interact correctly with each other. Example: Testing the integration between a payment gateway and an order management system.
3. System Testing: Verifies the complete integrated system as a whole to ensure compliance with the specified requirements.
4. Sanity Testing: A quick check to verify that a specific functionality or bug fix works as expected.
5. Smoke Testing: A high-level test performed after a new build to check whether the major functionalities of the application are working fine.
6. Regression Testing: Ensures that recent changes in the code have not adversely affected existing features.
7. User Acceptance Testing (UAT): Conducted by end-users or clients to confirm the system meets their needs and business goals.

B. Non-Functional Testing

This type focuses on how the system performs rather than what it does. It evaluates system attributes such as performance, usability, reliability, and scalability.

Common Types of Non-Functional Testing:

1. Performance Testing: Determines how the application performs under different loads.
2. Security Testing: Identifies vulnerabilities, data leaks, or threats in the system.
Example: Checking for SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and authentication flaws.
3. Usability Testing: Evaluates how user-friendly and intuitive the application is.
4. Compatibility Testing: Ensures the software works across different browsers, devices, operating systems, and network environments.
5. Scalability Testing: Verifies that the application can handle increasing loads without degradation.
6. Reliability and Recovery Testing: Checks the system’s ability to recover from crashes, failures, or unexpected interruptions.
7. Compliance Testing: Ensures the software adheres to industry regulations, standards, or legal requirements.

2. Based on Approach or Method

Testing can also be classified based on how it is performed.

A. Manual Testing

Testers execute test cases manually without using any automation tools.

• Suitable for exploratory, usability, and ad-hoc testing.
• Relies on human observation and judgment.
• Time-consuming but valuable in identifying user experience issues.

B. Automation Testing

Automation testing uses tools like Selenium, Cypress, Playwright, or TestNG to execute repetitive test cases automatically.

• Improves efficiency, accuracy, and test coverage.
• Especially useful for regression, performance, and load testing.
• Requires upfront effort to build and maintain scripts.

3. Based on Software Development Phase (Testing Levels)

Testing is performed at various levels during development.

1. Unit Testing: Conducted by developers to validate small code units.
2. Integration Testing: Ensures combined parts of the system work together.
3. System Testing: Conducted on the complete application to verify all end-to-end scenarios.
4. Acceptance Testing: Validates the entire system against business requirements before release.

4. Based on Test Objective

Some tests have specific objectives beyond functionality.

• Alpha Testing: Done internally by the development/testing team before release.
• Beta Testing: Done by external users to gather real-world feedback.
• Exploratory Testing: Testers explore the application without predefined test cases to uncover hidden defects.
• Ad-hoc Testing: Informal testing without documentation, often guided by intuition.
• Monkey Testing: Random testing to check system stability under unexpected inputs.

5. Based on Execution Environment

1. Black Box Testing: Tester focuses on input/output without knowing internal code structure. Example: Entering valid credentials to check login success.
2. White Box Testing: Tester examines the internal logic and structure of the code. Example: Testing code paths, loops, and conditions.
3. Gray Box Testing: Combines both black box and white box testing — the tester has partial knowledge of the internal structure.

6. Specialized Types of Testing

Certain domains require domain-specific or environment-specific testing:

• API Testing: Ensures APIs work as expected with proper responses, error codes, and data handling.
• Mobile Testing: Focuses on functionality, usability, and performance on mobile devices.
• Database Testing: Validates data integrity, consistency, and correctness in database operations.
• Localization and Internationalization Testing: Ensures the software adapts to different languages and regions correctly.

Conclusion

There is no one-size-fits-all testing approach — each type serves a unique purpose. In real-world projects, testers often combine multiple types to ensure thorough validation of the application.

Effective software testing ensures:

• The application works as expected.
• Performance and security are reliable.
• The user experience is smooth.
• The software meets business and customer expectations.

In summary:

Software testing is a broad discipline comprising many types — functional, non-functional, manual, automated, and specialized — all aimed at ensuring the final product is bug-free, reliable, and high-quality.

questions.question: What is Static and Dynamic testing?
questions.answer:
In software testing, the objective is to ensure that the software product is of high quality, free from defects, and meets business requirements. To achieve this, testing is broadly classified into two main categories — Static Testing and Dynamic Testing. Both serve different purposes and occur at different stages of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).

Static Testing

Static Testing is a type of software testing technique where the software is tested without executing the code. It focuses on reviewing and analyzing the artifacts of the project — such as requirements, design documents, and source code — to identify defects early in the development phase.

Key Characteristics:

• Performed in the early stages of SDLC.
• Does not require code execution.
• Focuses on prevention of defects rather than detection.
• Involves manual reviews, inspections, walkthroughs, or static analysis tools.

Examples of Artifacts Checked:

• Requirement Specification Documents (SRS, BRD)
• Design Documents
• Test Cases
• Source Code
• User Manuals

Common Static Testing Techniques:

1. Reviews: Informal examination of documents by peers or team members.
2. Walkthroughs: Author of the document leads the team through it to gather feedback.
3. Inspections: Formal, structured process with defined roles (moderator, author, reader).
4. Static Analysis Tools: Automated tools that analyze code for syntax errors, unused variables, coding standard violations, etc.

Advantages of Static Testing:

• Detects defects early, before execution.
• Reduces rework cost.
• Ensures adherence to coding and documentation standards.
• Improves overall software quality and maintainability.

Example:
During a code review, a tester or developer finds a logical error in an if-else condition before the code is executed. That is a classic example of static testing.

Dynamic Testing

Dynamic Testing is a testing technique that involves executing the code or software application to verify that it behaves as expected. This type of testing focuses on detecting defects in the actual running application by observing outputs, system behavior, and performance.

Key Characteristics:

• Conducted after code development.
• Requires code execution.
• Focuses on validation — checking that the system meets the requirements.
• Helps find runtime errors, logic defects, and performance issues.

Types of Dynamic Testing:

Dynamic Testing is broadly divided into two categories:

White-box Testing (Structural Testing):

• Tests internal logic, code structure, and program flow.
• Example: Unit testing, integration testing.

Black-box Testing (Functional Testing):

• Tests software based on inputs and expected outputs without knowledge of the code.
• Example: System testing, regression testing, user acceptance testing (UAT).

Examples of Dynamic Testing Techniques:

• Unit Testing
• Integration Testing
• System Testing
• Acceptance Testing
• Performance and Load Testing

Advantages of Dynamic Testing:

• Validates functional behavior of the software.
• Identifies runtime issues and unexpected system behavior.
• Ensures the software works correctly in real-world scenarios.
• Improves user satisfaction by verifying end-to-end functionality.

Example:
When a tester runs a login test case to verify whether valid credentials allow access to the dashboard, it involves dynamic testing, since the software is executed.

Key Differences Between Static and Dynamic Testing


Relationship Between the Two

Static and Dynamic testing are complementary to each other — not alternatives.

• Static Testing ensures the correctness of documentation and design, helping prevent defects before execution.
• Dynamic Testing ensures the application behaves correctly during execution and user interaction.

Together, they create a complete quality assurance strategy, improving efficiency, reducing cost, and delivering a robust final product.

Conclusion

Static Testing ensures the software is built correctly, while Dynamic Testing ensures the right software is built.

Both are essential in the software testing lifecycle to achieve a high-quality, reliable, and defect-free product. An effective testing process includes a combination of both techniques to detect defects early, validate behavior, and reduce time and cost in the long run.

questions.question: Selenium - Explain the WebDriver create statement?
questions.answer:
In Selenium automation, one of the most common and fundamental lines of code we write is the WebDriver creation statement — for example:

WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();

Even though it looks simple, this single line of code performs several important actions behind the scenes. Let’s break it down step by step to understand it fully.

1. WebDriver is an Interface

• In Selenium, WebDriver is an interface defined in the org.openqa.selenium package.
• Being an interface means it only contains method declarations such as get(), findElement(), click(), sendKeys(), etc., but no actual implementations.
• These methods define the contract for how automation scripts will interact with a browser — but not how each browser performs these operations.

Example methods in WebDriver interface:

void get(String url);
WebElement findElement(By by);
String getTitle();
void quit();

2. ChromeDriver is a Class (Implementation of WebDriver)

• ChromeDriver is a concrete class that implements the WebDriver interface.
• It provides the actual logic for controlling the Google Chrome browser.
• So when we create an object of ChromeDriver, it can perform the operations defined in WebDriver — such as opening a webpage, clicking a button, or extracting text.

The class is located in the package:
org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver

3. The Statement: WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();

Now, let’s dissect this line:

Left Side: WebDriver driver

• This declares a reference variable driver of type WebDriver (interface type).
• This means driver can hold a reference to any class object that implements WebDriver (e.g., ChromeDriver, FirefoxDriver, EdgeDriver).
• This is an example of polymorphism in Java — where a parent interface reference points to a child class object.
• The benefit is flexibility — if tomorrow you want to run your tests on Firefox, you can simply change:

WebDriver driver = new FirefoxDriver();
without modifying the rest of your code.

Right Side: new ChromeDriver()

• This creates an instance of the ChromeDriver class.
• When the ChromeDriver object is created, Selenium launches a new instance of the Chrome browser.
• Behind the scenes, the ChromeDriver class starts the chromedriver.exe server (a standalone executable that acts as a bridge between Selenium commands and Chrome browser).
• It communicates via the JSON Wire Protocol or W3C WebDriver protocol to send and receive commands.

4. Putting it all together

So, the statement:
WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();
can be explained as:

• Declare a WebDriver reference variable (driver).
• Instantiate the ChromeDriver class (which implements WebDriver).
• Launch a new Chrome browser window.
• Assign that browser control to the reference variable driver.
• Now, driver can be used to perform browser actions such as:

5. Example with Other Browsers

WebDriver driver = new FirefoxDriver(); // Launches Mozilla Firefox
WebDriver driver = new EdgeDriver();    // Launches Microsoft Edge
WebDriver driver = new SafariDriver();  // Launches Safari (on macOS)

All of these work because they implement the same WebDriver interface — which ensures your test code remains consistent across browsers.

6. WebDriverManager (Optional Modern Usage)

In earlier Selenium versions, we had to manually set the driver path using:

System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "path/to/chromedriver.exe");

Now, with WebDriverManager, this is automated:

WebDriverManager.chromedriver().setup();
WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();

It automatically downloads the compatible driver binary and configures the system path — making the setup cleaner and faster.

7. Summary


Final Explanation

The statement WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); creates an object of ChromeDriver (which implements WebDriver) and assigns it to a WebDriver interface reference. It opens a Chrome browser instance and enables us to automate browser actions using Selenium’s WebDriver methods. This approach follows Java’s polymorphism principle, allowing easy switching between browsers without changing the core test logic.

questions.question: What's your approach to Test coverage while writing Test cases for any functionality?
questions.answer:
When writing test cases for any functionality, my approach to achieving comprehensive test coverage involves a structured and layered process that ensures all aspects of the feature—functional, non-functional, positive, negative, and edge cases—are validated. The goal is not just to test that the system works, but to ensure that it behaves correctly in all scenarios, including unexpected ones.

1. Understand Requirements Thoroughly

The foundation of good test coverage starts with a deep understanding of the requirements or user stories:

• I review Business Requirement Documents (BRD), Functional Specifications, and Acceptance Criteria.
• I identify both explicit requirements (clearly mentioned) and implicit ones (inferred from business logic or user expectations).
• If there are any ambiguities, I clarify them early with the BA, Product Owner, or Developer to avoid gaps later.

Example: If a login functionality is described, I don’t just test “valid login.” I also identify areas like password rules, error messages, lockout scenarios, and security checks.

2. Identify Test Scenarios and Conditions

Next, I break the functionality into logical scenarios and sub-flows:

• Main flow (happy path) — The core expected behavior.
• Alternate flows — Variations that still represent valid user behavior.
• Exceptional flows — How the system behaves when something goes wrong.

I often use flowcharts or mind maps to visualize how different paths connect, which helps ensure no path is left untested.

Example: For a payment module, I’d map out flows like:

• Successful payment
• Payment declined due to insufficient funds
• Payment canceled mid-way
• Network timeout or session expiry

3. Apply Test Design Techniques

To achieve structured coverage and avoid redundancy, I use formal test design techniques such as:

• Equivalence Partitioning (EP): Dividing input data into valid and invalid partitions.
• Boundary Value Analysis (BVA): Focusing on edge conditions where most defects occur.
• Decision Table Testing: For complex business rules involving multiple conditions.
• State Transition Testing: For systems that behave differently based on previous states.
• Error Guessing: Using domain knowledge to anticipate likely failure points.

These techniques ensure both breadth (covering all functional areas) and depth (covering variations within each area) of coverage.

4. Include Different Test Types

To ensure end-to-end coverage, I include multiple test types:

• Positive tests: Verify that the system works as expected under normal conditions.
• Negative tests: Check how the system handles invalid, missing, or out-of-range inputs.
• Boundary tests: Validate limits and thresholds.
• UI tests: Verify field alignments, error messages, labels, etc.
• Security and validation tests: For login, authentication, and access control.
• Integration tests: To ensure smooth data flow between modules or systems.

5. Traceability to Requirements

To ensure nothing is missed, I maintain a Requirement Traceability Matrix (RTM):

• Each test case is mapped to one or more requirement IDs.
• This helps verify that every requirement has at least one corresponding test.
• It also helps during regression testing and impact analysis when a change request is raised.

Outcome: 100% functional coverage can be demonstrated and verified.

6. Consider Real-World and Edge Scenarios

I always include real-world usage conditions:

• Testing with large datasets, invalid data formats, or long text inputs.
• Multi-user or concurrent usage scenarios.
• Different browsers, devices, or environments (if applicable).

These help catch issues that might not appear in straightforward test conditions but occur frequently in production.

7. Review and Peer Feedback

Once the test cases are drafted:

• I conduct a peer review or walkthrough session with other QA members and sometimes developers.
• This helps identify missing scenarios and improves test clarity and maintainability.

8. Prioritize and Optimize

If time or resources are limited, I prioritize test cases based on:

• Business impact
• Risk level
• Complexity of functionality
• Frequency of use

This ensures that the most critical paths are always covered first.

9. Measure Coverage

Finally, I measure test coverage using:

• Requirement coverage (via RTM)
• Code coverage (for automation tests, if applicable)
• Defect coverage (ensuring all defect areas are retested and verified)
• Risk coverage (ensuring all high-risk areas have sufficient tests)

These metrics help in identifying areas that need more attention or improvement.

Example Summary

For a “Login Functionality,” my test coverage approach would include:

• Valid and invalid credentials
• Empty username/password
• SQL injection attempts
• Account lock after multiple failures
• Password expiry
• Remember me / session timeout
• Browser compatibility
• API response and error handling

This ensures complete coverage from function

questions.question: What is Boundary value analysis and Equivalence partitioning?
questions.answer:
Boundary Value Analysis (BVA) and Equivalence Partitioning (EP) are two fundamental test design techniques used in software testing to improve coverage, efficiency, and effectiveness of test cases. Both are black-box testing methods that focus on input conditions and help testers design test scenarios without having to exhaustively test every possible input.

1. Equivalence Partitioning (EP)

Definition: Equivalence Partitioning is a technique where the input data of a software application is divided into different groups or partitions (called equivalence classes) based on similar behavior. The assumption is that if one value from a partition works correctly, then all other values in that partition are expected to behave the same way.

Purpose:

• To reduce the total number of test cases while still achieving maximum coverage.
• To ensure that all possible input scenarios are represented through representative values.

Example: Let’s say a field accepts age input between 18 and 60.

• Valid Partition: 18 to 60 (e.g., pick 25 as a representative test value).
• Invalid Partitions:
• Less than 18 (e.g., 10)
• Greater than 60 (e.g., 70) So instead of testing every possible age, we just select representative values from each partition.

2. Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)

Definition: Boundary Value Analysis focuses on testing the values at the edges (boundaries) of input ranges rather than the values within the partitions. Since defects are more likely to occur at the boundaries, this technique helps in identifying issues that occur at the limits of input ranges.

Purpose:

• To detect errors at the “edge cases” where software often fails.
• To complement Equivalence Partitioning by validating both valid and invalid boundary conditions.

Example: Using the same age input (18 to 60) example:

• Test the lower boundary: 17 (just below), 18 (exact boundary), and 19 (just above).
• Test the upper boundary: 59 (just below), 60 (exact boundary), and 61 (just above).

This ensures all possible edge cases are validated.

3. Difference Between EP and BVA


4. How They Work Together

• Equivalence Partitioning ensures that every category of input (valid and invalid) is tested at least once.
• Boundary Value Analysis ensures that the critical edge conditions of these partitions are tested.
• Together, they provide strong coverage with fewer test cases compared to exhaustive testing.

5. Real-Life Example

Suppose you’re testing a login form with a password field that must be between 6 and 12 characters:

EP Tests:

• Valid partition → Any password with 6–12 characters (e.g., "mypwd123").
• Invalid partitions → Fewer than 6 (e.g., "abc") and more than 12 (e.g., "verylongpassword123").

BVA Tests:

• Just below the lower boundary (5 characters → "abcde").
• At the lower boundary (6 characters → "abcdef").
• Just above the lower boundary (7 characters → "abcdefg").
• Just below the upper boundary (11 characters).
• At the upper boundary (12 characters).
• Just above the upper boundary (13 characters).

This ensures robust validation of the field.

Final Summary (Interview Style)

“Equivalence Partitioning and Boundary Value Analysis are black-box testing techniques used to design efficient test cases. EP helps by dividing input data into valid and invalid partitions and picking representative values, while BVA focuses on testing the boundary conditions where defects are more likely to occur. For example, if a field accepts ages between 18 and 60, EP would test a few representative values like 25, 10, and 70, while BVA would specifically test 17, 18, 19, 59, 60, and 61. Together, they ensure comprehensive coverage with minimal test cases.”

questions.question: How do you resolve Conflicts in Git?
questions.answer:
When working with Git — especially in collaborative environments where multiple people are modifying the same codebase — merge conflicts are quite common. Understanding how to detect, analyze, and resolve them effectively is a key skill for any developer or automation tester using Git.

1. What is a Git Conflict?

A Git conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically merge changes from different branches because the same part of a file has been changed in multiple places.

This typically happens when:

• Two developers edit the same lines in a file.
• One developer edits a file that another developer deleted.
• One developer renames a file while another modifies it.
• Changes from two branches overlap and Git can’t decide which version to keep.

Git tries to merge changes automatically, but when it finds competing edits that can’t be merged safely, it marks the file as “conflicted” and pauses the merge until you manually resolve it.

2. When Do Conflicts Occur?

Conflicts can arise in several scenarios:

• During a Merge: (When integrating one branch into another.)
git merge feature-branch
• During a Rebase: (When replaying your branch commits on top of another branch.)
git rebase main
• During a Pull: (If the remote branch and your local branch have both diverged.)
git pull

3. Example Scenario

Imagine you have two branches:
• main
• feature-login

In main:
System.out.println("Welcome to the Application!");

In feature-login:
System.out.println("Welcome, please log in to continue!");

Now, when you try to merge feature-login into main, Git sees that both branches changed the same line, and it doesn’t know which one to keep — resulting in a merge conflict.

4. How Git Indicates Conflicts

Git will:

• Stop the merge process.
• Mark the conflicted file in your working directory.
• Add conflict markers inside the file.

Example conflict in a file:
<<<<<<< HEAD
System.out.println("Welcome to the Application!");
=======
System.out.println("Welcome, please log in to continue!");
>>>>>>> feature-login

Meaning:

• The code between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= represents your current branch’s code.
• The code between ======= and >>>>>>> branch-name represents the incoming branch’s code.

5. Steps to Resolve Git Conflicts

Here’s the standard and professional way to resolve conflicts:

Step 1: Identify Conflicted Files

Run:
git status

Git will show which files have conflicts under:
Unmerged paths:
  both modified:   src/Main.java

Step 2: Open the Conflicted File

Open the file in your preferred IDE or text editor. You’ll see conflict markers as shown earlier.

Step 3: Manually Resolve the Conflict

• Decide which change to keep — yours, theirs, or a combination.
• Edit the file to remove conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>).
• Modify the code to the final version you want.

Example resolved file:
System.out.println("Welcome! Please log in to continue!");

Step 4: Mark Conflict as Resolved

Once you’ve fixed all conflicts, add the resolved file:
git add src/Main.java

Step 5: Complete the Merge or Rebase

If you were merging:
git commit
Git will open the default editor for a merge commit message — save and exit.

If you were rebasing:
git rebase --continue

Step 6: Verify

After committing, check the status again:
git status

It should show no pending conflicts, and you can proceed with pushing your code.

6. Tips for Avoiding Conflicts

1. Pull frequently: Always pull the latest code before starting new work to minimize drift.
2. Commit often, but meaningfully: Smaller, focused commits make it easier to merge changes.
3. Communicate with teammates: Inform others if you’re modifying shared or sensitive areas of the codebase.
4. Use rebase carefully: Rebasing changes commit history — use it only on your personal feature branches.
5. Use good Git practices: Avoid editing the same files as others unnecessarily. Resolve conflicts locally before pushing to shared branches.

7. Conflict Resolution Tools

Modern IDEs and Git tools simplify this process:

• Visual Studio Code: Built-in merge conflict editor.
• IntelliJ / Eclipse: Highlight conflicts visually.
• GitHub / GitLab UI: Allows resolving small conflicts directly in the web interface.

Command Line Tools:

• git mergetool opens a visual merge tool.
• Example: git mergetool

8. Example: Using Git Commands

Here’s a full example:

# Step 1: Merge branch
git merge feature/login

# Step 2: See conflicts
git status

# Step 3: Open and fix conflicts
vim src/LoginPage.java

# Step 4: Add resolved files
git add src/LoginPage.java

# Step 5: Commit merge
git commit -m "Resolved merge conflict in LoginPage.java"

# Step 6: Push changes
git push origin main

9. Summary Table


10. Final Summary Answer

A Git conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically merge changes between branches. To resolve it, you need to identify the conflicted files using git status, manually edit the conflict markers to choose or combine changes, add the resolved files using git add, and then complete the merge with git commit. Tools like VS Code or IntelliJ can make this process easier. The key is frequent pulls, good communication, and small, isolated commits to avoid major conflicts.

questions.question: TestNG - What does `threadPoolSize` mean, and how does it work?
questions.answer:
In TestNG, the threadPoolSize attribute is used to enable parallel execution of test methods within the same <test> tag or class. It defines how many threads should be allocated to run a particular test method concurrently, which helps improve execution speed—especially for time-consuming or independent test cases.

Definition:

threadPoolSize is an attribute used in the @Test annotation of TestNG to specify the number of threads that will be used to execute a test method in parallel.

Syntax:

@Test(threadPoolSize = 3, invocationCount = 6, timeOut = 10000)
public void testMethod() {
    System.out.println("Thread ID: " + Thread.currentThread().getId());
}

How it Works:

By default, TestNG runs tests sequentially—one after another. However, when you specify threadPoolSize along with invocationCount, TestNG runs multiple instances of the same test method at the same time in different threads.

Let’s understand the above example:

• invocationCount = 6: means the method will be executed 6 times.
• threadPoolSize = 3: means TestNG will create a pool of 3 threads to run those 6 executions.
• Hence, at any given time, 3 threads will be executing the method in parallel until all 6 invocations complete.

So, the method executions will be divided like this:

• 3 methods run first (using 3 threads)
• Once a thread finishes, it picks up the next pending invocation
• Total 6 executions will finish in 2 cycles (since 6 ÷ 3 = 2)

Important Rules:

1. Must be used with invocationCount — threadPoolSize only makes sense when a test method is invoked multiple times. If you specify threadPoolSize without invocationCount, TestNG will throw an exception.
2. Each thread runs a separate instance of the test method. This means instance variables are not shared between threads, which helps prevent data inconsistency issues.
3. Parallelism scope — This only controls parallel execution within a test method, not across multiple classes or test tags. To achieve class-level or suite-level parallelism, you use the <suite parallel="classes" thread-count="x"> configuration in testng.xml.

Practical Example:

Suppose you have a test that simulates multiple user logins to check system performance under load:

@Test(threadPoolSize = 5, invocationCount = 10, timeOut = 20000)
public void simulateUserLogin() {
    System.out.println("Running Thread: " + Thread.currentThread().getId());
    // Code to simulate login

}
• 10 login simulations will occur.
• 5 threads will be created.
• 5 logins will run in parallel, then the next 5 will start once a thread is free.
• The total time will be roughly half of the sequential execution time (depending on CPU capacity).

Benefits in Test Automation:

1. Reduces total execution time — Especially useful when tests are independent (like API calls or parallel browser sessions).
2. Simulates real-world scenarios — Such as multiple users accessing an application simultaneously.
3. Improves resource utilization — TestNG utilizes CPU cores efficiently by distributing workload.

Common Use Cases:

• Load testing or concurrency simulation (e.g., multiple logins)
• Running independent test methods in parallel
• Executing data-driven tests where each dataset is independent

Things to Watch Out For:

• Thread safety: Avoid using shared static variables or non-synchronized resources inside parallel tests.
• External resources: Database or file access may cause race conditions if not handled properly.
• System load: Too high a thread count may lead to CPU overload or network timeouts.
• Debugging complexity: Parallel execution can make logs harder to trace.

Example Output (illustration):

Thread ID: 11
Thread ID: 12
Thread ID: 13
Thread ID: 11
Thread ID: 12
Thread ID: 13

This output confirms that the same method was executed multiple times across 3 threads.

Summary:


In short:

The threadPoolSize attribute in TestNG enables parallel execution of the same test method across multiple threads, improving execution efficiency and mimicking real-world concurrent user behavior — but it must be used carefully with invocationCount to avoid synchronization issues.

What's new with Selenium v-4?
questions.answer:
W3C compliance of WebDriver APIs
In Selenium’s earlier versions (i.e., Selenium 3), the JSON Wire Protocol was responsible for communication between the web browser and the test code. This led to the additional overhead of encoding and decoding the API requests using the W3C protocol.

A significant change under the hood for WebDriver is the complete W3C compliance of the WebDriver APIs. This standardization will eliminate the need for encoding and decoding the API requests by the JSON wire protocol for communication between browsers and test scripts. This means the WebDriver will now interact directly with the target browser. This standardization will result in more stable cross browser tests. In a nutshell, JSON wire protocol is deprecated in Selenium.

Enhanced Selenium Grid
No longer be any need to set up and start hubs and nodes separately. Teams can now deploy the grid in three modes: Standalone mode, Hub and Node, fully distributed. The Grid will now support IPV6 addresses, and users can communicate with the Grid using the HTTPS protocol. It would be much easier to use configuration files as users can configure the Grid using human-understandable TOML (Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language) language.

The new Selenium Grid comes with Docker support. This will enable developers or testers to spin up the containers rather than setting up heavy virtual machines. Moreover, it is redesigned in a way that will allow QAs to deploy the grid on Kubernetes for better scaling.

Upgraded Selenium IDE
With Selenium 4, the IDE is revived and improved.

questions.question: How do you plan resourcing?
questions.answer: Resourcing, i.e., in simple terms how many people are required for how many days to deliver a product. The first pre-requisite to resource-planning is estimation. Say the total effort estimation comes to around 150PDs, i.e., 150 Person-days. A single person would take 150 working days to deliver the product. The second pre-requisite to resource-planning is the timelines. Say the project timelines are for a month, i.e., the product needs to be delivered in a month's time. 20-working days. Combining both estimations & timelines, A single person would take 150 days. But we want it delivered in 20 days. The calculation says we need 150/20 = 7.5 people to deliver. Adding buffer as risk contingency, we need 8 people to deliver a product estimated at 150 PDs in a month's time. Tip: It's not that easy though. Multiple other factors come into play — third-parties, systems involved, test automation, timelines, methodology being followed, etc.

questions.question: What you will do if you have conflict with your manager on attitude or any other opinion?

Employee thinks Manager is clever/shrewd, Manager think employee has attitude problems. I guess "communication-to-understand" is the only key. Beta testers (client users or set of actual end-users) try the software, use it consistently for a specific period of time and report back any issues, bugs or feedback about it. For the given problem statement, there can be multiple reasons — e No binding: just a show-piece button with no corresponding binding to trigger any action. e Javascript failure: The associated Javascript validation fails silently without throwing any errors. e HTML/CSS Issue: The button is clickable only at certain dimensions OR not interactable at all. e Browser-compatibility: Tech-stack used isn't working with older browser versions/specific browser. e Pre-requisites: Say it's a flash object and it isn't enabled on your machine. Or say Javascript execution is disabled. o Firewall/Security/Blockers: Some security software or firewall settings are blocking the call-to-action. Some browser add-on you installed might be blocking the click. e Cache/Browser refresh: Some cache entries disallowing button click. questions.question: The QA team starts testing a software/product and there are "way too many" defects. Every other scenario is failing, new flows are explored & clarifications sought. What would be the strategy now?

questions.question: What if Developers reject your defects and you are able to reproduce it on your machine?

Most of the times, developers reject a bug because it is not reproducible on their system.
